paper.title_en: The Stellar-Mass Dependence of Feedback-Driven Outflows in DESI DR1 Star-Forming Galaxies
paper.abstract_en: Stellar feedback plays a key role in regulating star formation and shaping the evolution of star-forming galaxies. Low-mass galaxies provide one of the most powerful laboratories for testing stellar feedback and its impact on galaxy evolution. Numerical simulations predict that repeated feedback-driven gas inflows and outflows generate a "breathing mode," producing a positive correlation between mass-normalized gas velocity dispersion and recent star formation in dwarf galaxies. Whether this kinematic signature persists at higher stellar masses has remained untested. We investigate this question using $\sim1200$ star-forming galaxies with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectroscopy and COSMOS2020 photometry spanning $7.9<\log M_\star/M_\odot<11.5$ within $z<0.25$. Ionized-gas kinematics are measured with pPXF, and recent star formation histories are reconstructed through joint spectrophotometric fitting with Prospector. We confirm the predicted positive correlation throughout the low-mass regime with $\log M_\star/M_\odot \lesssim 9.8$, quantitatively consistent with previous observations and FIRE-2 simulations. Above $\log M_\star/M_\odot \sim 9.8$, the correlation weakens rapidly and becomes consistent with zero, providing the first empirical constraint on the stellar mass scale above which the kinematic signature of feedback-driven outflow cycles becomes negligible. Our results establish a characteristic stellar mass above which stellar feedback no longer dominates galaxy-scale gas kinematics, providing a new observational benchmark for models of feedback-regulated galaxy evolution. Future joint analyses of gas kinematics and stellar structure will test whether this transition is accompanied by the broader galaxy response predicted by the breathing mode scenario.
